newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Filipino drivers set to pay more at the pumps.
newsitem.headline: Filipino drivers set to pay more at the pumps.

text.p: Filipino drivers will pay more at the pumps from Saturday as the country's oil industry is freed of government controls, but petroleum product prices on average will be lower, oil companies said.
The country's three major oil refiners announced price changes on Friday in the face of accusations that the deregulation will lead to a sharp price increase.

Petron Corp, Pilipinas Shell Petroleum Corp and Caltex Philippines Inc said they would raise the price of premium gasoline, unleaded premium gasoline and liquefied petroleum gas while reducing those of regular gas, jet fuel, kerosene, diesel and fuel oil.
Petron and Caltex said overall posted prices of wholesale products would be cut by an average of one centavo per litre.

"We were looking at Petron before we make our own adjustments. We were earlier planning to raise prices by an average of five to six centavos but with Petron's announcement, we couldn't go above its price or else we will lose customers," a source at Caltex told Reuters.

The three oil refiners raised their prices for premium gasoline by an average of 41.45 centavos per litre to 11.30 pesos ($0.43) and for unleaded gasoline an average of 0.66 centavos to 10.8986 pesos per litre.
They raised the price of liquefied petroleum gas by an average of 62.40 centavos to 7.825 pesos per litre.
Energy Regulatory Board (ERB) chairman Bayani Faylona said the oil industry would now freely determine petroleum prices under the full deregulation set-up.
The ERB has set petroleum prices for 25 years.

"But as far as I know, the oil companies are not going to make any drastic changes. They would like to show the public that they are not going to take advantage of full deregulation by increasing prices unreasonably," Faylona added.
He also said that before regulation began in the early 1970s, Philippine petroleum prices were among the world's lowest.
Pilipinas Shell president Reinier Willems told Reuters earlier this week that in the medium and long term, there would likely be price wars among industry players.

Four opposition congressmen along with three human rights groups filed a petition with the Supreme Court on Thursday to halt the deregulation. The court has yet to make a decision on whether to issue a temporary restraining order.

One group, the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), or the New Patriotic Alliance, started a two-day protest rally in front of the offices of the three oil companies in Manila's financial district of Makati on Friday. A night vigil and march near the presidential palace would also be held.

"Our opposition to oil deregulation is unequivocal. This will only lead to cartelisation and even if they claim that new entrants will guard against cartels, these minor players will not be a match for the established oil companies," Nathanael Santiago, a Bayan official, told Reuters.
The government has taken the criticism in its stride.
"When we were regulating they were complaining every time we fixed prices. Now that we are deregulating, they are also complaining. What can I say?" Faylona said.
